claim: Lineage regulates the synaptic connections between neurons in some regions of the invertebrate nervous system.

evidence: This is a general statement supported by citations to prior work in the field.

claim: In the Drosophila olfactory system, projection neurons are specified by cell lineage to receive synaptic input from the axons of specific types of olfactory sensory neurons (OSNs).
source: For example, in the Drosophila olfactory system, projection neurons are specified by cell lineage to receive synaptic input from the axons of specific types of olfactory sensory neurons (OSNs) (Jefferis et al., 2001; Li et al., 2018).

claim: Each OSN expresses just one of more than one thousand odorant receptors.
source: Each OSN expresses just one of more than one thousand odorant receptors (Buck and Axel, 1991; Chess et al., 1994).

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: In mammals, the majority (>90%) of M/T cells have a single apical dendrite that branches into a single glomerulus.
source: In mammals, the majority (>90%) of M/T cells have a single apical dendrite that branches into a single glomerulus (Mori, 1987; Shepherd, 1990; Malun and Brunjes, 1996)

claim: M/T cells receive sensory input from OSNs expressing a particular odor receptor in the glomerulus.

claim: Lineage does not determine the sensory input of the OB projection neurons.

evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by experimental data.

source: and suggest that the connectivity between OB projection neurons and olfactory sensory neurons depends on other mechanisms, including random targeting of dendrites towards glomeruli and activity-dependent mechanisms.

claim: M/T cells originate from progenitors located in the OB primordium, which is derived from the rostral part of the dorsal telencephalon.
source: M/T cells originate from progenitors located in the OB primordium, which is derived from the rostral part of the dorsal telencephalon (Hinds, 1968a; Hinds, 1968b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Nestin-CreERT2 can be used to activate Cre in neuronal progenitors in a sparse manner.

evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Nestin-CreERT2::Confetti mice did not label any neurons in the brain without tamoxifen (TMX) administration.
source: First, we confirmed that our transgenic mice Nestin-CreERT2::Confetti did not label any neurons in the brain without tamoxifen (TMX) administration (n = 3; data not shown).

claim: An injection of 1 mg of TMX per 40 g of body weight into a 10-day pregnant female (E10.5) resulted in around 20 M/T cells labeled in the OB when the brains were examined at postnatal day 21 (P21).
source: Second, we found that with an injection of 1 mg of TMX per 40 g of body weight into a 10-day pregnant female (E10.5) we observed a handful of labeled pyramidal neuron clones in the neocortex, and around 20 M/T cells labeled in the OB when the brains were examined at postnatal day 21 (P21) (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study.

claim: Between none to a single progenitor was labeled per fluorescent protein in the OB primordium (n = 6 embryos) when animals were analyzed 2 days after TMX administration (E12.5).
source: With these conditions, we observed between none to a single progenitor labeled per fluorescent protein in the OB primordium (n = 6 embryos), the presumptive location of the M/T progenitors.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study.

claim: Any group of M/T cells labeled with the same fluorescent protein in the OB are assumed to be part of a single clone.
source: However, because of the low number of clones labeled with these conditions we will work under the assumption that any group of M/T cells labeled with the same fluorescent protein in the OB are part of a single clone.
evidence: This is an assumption made by the authors based on their experimental conditions.

claim: E10.5 is the peak time for mitral cell generation.
source: To study the lineage of the M/T cells we induced Cre activity at E10.5, the peak time for mitral cell generation (Hinds, 1968a; Hinds, 1968b; Blanchart et al., 2006; Kim et al., 2011; Imamura et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: At P21, M/T cells have completed the refinement of their dendrites and they have a mature morphology with a single apical dendrite projecting into a single glomerulus.
source: Brains were analyzed at P21, once M/T cells have completed the refinement of their dendrites and they have a mature morphology with a single apical dendrite projecting into a single glomerulus (Figure 1A) (Malun and Brunjes, 1996; Lin et al., 2000; Matsutani and Yamamoto, 2000; Blanchart et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Many clones in the OB were labeled by RFP (n = 9), whereas YFP (n = 4) and CFP (n = 1) clones appeared less frequently.
source: Consistent with previous works, we observed that many clones in the OB were labeled by RFP (n = 9), whereas YFP (n = 4) and CFP (n = 1) clones appeared less frequently (Reeves et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study, consistent with prior work.

claim: 28 OBs were analyzed in total.
source: In total, we analyzed 28 OBs.

source: 15 of them did not have any labeled M/T cells.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study.

source: 11 OBs had both M and T cells labeled (n = 14 clones).

source: Two OBs had clones that contained only M cells (n = 2 clones).

claim: The average OB clone contained 22.14 ± 6.61 M/T cells (average ± standard deviation).
source: We found 310 labeled M/T cells in 14 putative clones in the OB, such that the average OB clone contained 22.14 ± 6.61 M/T cells (average ± standard deviation).

claim: The average cortical clone contained 92.67 ± 23.18 pyramidal neurons (average ± standard deviation).
source: We found 556 labeled cells in six neocortex clones, such that the average cortical clone contained 92.67 ± 23.18 pyramidal neurons (average ± standard deviation), consistent with previous results (Franco et al., 2012; Gao et al., 2014) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data, consistent with prior work.

claim: The clone size in the neocortex is approximately four times larger than in the OB.
source: These observations suggest that the clone size in the neocortex is approximately four times larger than in the OB, consistent with the previous results (Cárdenas et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data, consistent with prior work.

claim: Sister M/T cells were more separated from each other (287.47 µm ± 61.23; average ± standard deviation) than sister pyramidal neurons (59.56 µm ± 9.86).
source: We found that sister M/T cells were more separated from each other (287.47 µm ± 61.23; average ± standard deviation) than sister pyramidal neurons (59.56 µm ± 9.86) (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data.

claim: The dispersion of sister M/T cells observed is consistent with the tangential migration of immature M/T cells reported in the embryonic OB.
source: The dispersion of sister M/T cells that we observed is consistent with the tangential migration of immature M/T cells reported in the embryonic OB (Blanchart et al., 2006; Imamura et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data in the context of prior work.

claim: The NNDs between clonally related neurons were shorter than the simulated random datasets both for the OB and neocortex.
source: We found that the NNDs between clonally related neurons were shorter than the simulated random datasets both for the OB and neocortex (Figure 3E, p<0.01; two-way ANOVA).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Although sister M/T cells are not obviously clustered, their distribution in the OB is not random.
source: This indicates that although sister M/T cells are not obviously clustered, their distribution in the OB is not random.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The tangential migration of immature M/T cells in the embryonic OB may be regulated by gradients of secreted or cell adhesion molecules, biasing their distribution to specific regions within the OB.
source: Interestingly, previous works have observed that the tangential migration of immature M/T cells in the embryonic OB may be regulated by gradients of secreted (Inokuchi et al., 2017) or cell adhesion molecules (Bastakis et al., 2015), biasing their distribution to specific regions within the OB.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Migration of M/T cells is biased toward the dorsal or ventral regions of the OB at different developmental times.
source: Previous experiments have demonstrated that migration of M/T cells is biased toward the dorsal or ventral regions of the OB at different developmental times (Imamura et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: It has been hypothesized that the dorsal and ventral domains of the OB may have a preference to process innate and learned odorants, respectively.
source: In addition, it has been hypothesized that the dorsal and ventral domains of the OB may have a preference to process innate and learned odorants, respectively (Kobayakawa et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: When all the clones were analyzed together, there were no preferences in the distribution of M/T cells towards the dorsal or ventral domains.
source: Overall, when all the clones were analyzed together, there were no preferences in the distribution of M/T cells towards the dorsal or ventral domains (Figure 3—figure supplement 1L; p=0.67, t-test).

claim: No bias was detected for the distribution of M/T cells OB in the lateral or medial domains.
source: Similarly, we did not detect any bias for the distribution of M/T cells OB in the lateral or medial domains (data not shown).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study.

claim: In the neocortex the number of neurons per clone is reduced as progenitors are labeled at later embryonic stages.
source: Previous works have demonstrated that in the neocortex the number of neurons per clone is reduced as progenitors are labeled at later embryonic stages (Angevine and Sidman, 1961; Walsh and Cepko, 1988; Luskin et al., 1988; Price and Thurlow, 1988; Rakic, 1988; Gao et al., 2014).

claim: The clones that were labeled at E12.5 in the OBs contained fewer cells than at E10.5: 8.44 ± 6.37 M/T cells per clone (average ± standard deviation, n = 76 cells) when labeled at E12.5, compared with 22.14 ± 6.61 M/T cells per clone when labeled at E10.5.
source: Consistent with this observation, the clones that were labeled at E12.5 in the OBs contained fewer cells than at E10.5: 8.44 ± 6.37 M/T cells per clone (average ± standard deviation, n = 76 cells) when labeled at E12.5, compared with 22.14 ± 6.61 M/T cells per clone when labeled at E10.5 (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B, C-I').
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data.

claim: A reduction in the number of cells per clone in the neocortex was observed when labeling progenitors at later developmental stages (22.5 ± 6.47 pyramidal neurons (n = 135 cells) at E12.5 versus 92.67 ± 23.18 pyramidal neurons at E10.5).
source: Similarly, we observed a reduction in the number of cells per clone in the neocortex when labeling progenitors at later developmental stages (22.5 ± 6.47 pyramidal neurons (n = 135 cells) at E12.5 versus 92.67 ± 23.18 pyramidal neurons at E10.5)), consistent with previous results (Franco et al., 2012; Gao et al., 2014) (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B,K–P).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data, consistent with prior work.

claim: AOB M/T cells are born earlier than MOB M/T cells.
source: When TMX was administered at E12.5, we did not find any M/T cells labeled in the AOB, consistent with the observation that AOB M/T cells are born earlier than MOB M/T cells (Hinds, 1968a).

source: We inspected 28 OBs labeled at E10.5, and found that 10 OBs contained 18 M/T cells labeled in the AOB, with only 1–3 labeled M/T cells per AOB.

source: Although these small numbers do not allow for a definitive conclusion, our results suggest that there are separate progenitors for the M/T cells in the MOB and AOB.

source: It has been proposed that the anatomical organization of the OB may be analogous to the neocortex columnar organization.

source: In the neocortex it is thought that the pyramidal neurons forming part of a column perform a similar task (Rakic, 1988; Mountcastle, 1997).

source: Among all the labeled M/T cells that we detected (310 cells from 14 putative M/T clones (E10.5) and 74 cells from nine putative M/T clones (E12.5)), we never observed two neurons innervating the same glomerulus, even when their cell bodies were near each other (Figure 4B–E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).

source: This scenario could be expected for putative glomeruli responsive to relevant odors for survival, such as those responsive to predators or poisons, which require an innate and hardwired response of avoidance (Kobayakawa et al., 2007; Sosulski et al., 2011).

claim: Glomeruli in the AOB are less well defined and more difficult to identify than in the MOB.
source: Although glomeruli are clearly distinct in the MOB, glomeruli in the AOB are less well defined and more difficult to identify.

source: Although the small number of labeled AOB M/T cells does not allow us to draw any firm conclusions, we did not find any M/T cells whose apical dendrites innervated the same glomerulus (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), similar to what we observed in the MOB.

claim: Lineage does not determinate the input connectivity of the apical dendrites of projection neurons in the mammalian OB.
source: In summary, our results indicate that lineage does not determinate the input connectivity of the apical dendrites of projection neurons in the mammalian OB.

source: Our results indicate that the sensory input received by M/T cells is regulated by other factors independent of lineage, including random targeting of dendrites towards glomeruli and activity-dependent mechanisms, consistent with previous observations from multiple lines of evidence.

claim: During early postnatal stages M/T cells have several dendrites (between 3 to 5), and each of these dendrites project into different glomeruli that are close to each other, and immediately above their cell bodies.
source: First, during early postnatal stages M/T cells have several dendrites (between 3 to 5), and each of these dendrites project into different glomeruli that are close to each other, and immediately above their cell bodies (Hinds, 1968a; Blanchart et al., 2006).

source: Starting approximately 1 week after birth, a process of refinement occurs such that around 90% of M/T cells retain just one apical dendrite and retract all others, and that remaining single apical dendrite branches into a single glomerulus (Malun and Brunjes, 1996; Lin et al., 2000; Matsutani and Yamamoto, 2000; Blanchart et al., 2006).

source: Interestingly, the refinement by which M/T cells retain a single dendrite is a process partially dependent on neuronal activity.

source: Olfactory deprivation by naris occlusion retards the refinement of M/T cell dendrites by approximately one week, although eventually the refinement process is accomplished to the same degree as in non-manipulated animals (Matsutani and Yamamoto, 2000).

source: Interestingly, a recent work demonstrated that genetic blocking of action potentials in M/T cells prevented the dendrite refinement process such that even in adult animals the majority of M/T cells have several dendrites projecting into multiple glomeruli (Fujimoto et al., 2019).

source: Finally, recent experiments indicate that activity-dependent mechanisms can direct the projection of M/T cell dendrites into specific glomeruli.

source: For example, sensory odor experience in utero recruits the apical dendrites of M/T cells to the activated glomeruli (Liu et al., 2016).

source: Similarly, genetic ablation of a large set of OSNs results in the absence of a large number of glomeruli in the dorsal OB, and in these animals, some M/T cells located in those regions lacking glomeruli extend their dendrites tangentially for a long distance until they reach a region with glomeruli, where they branch (Nishizumi et al., 2019).

claim: M/T cells are not committed to project into specific glomeruli.

source: Instead, the available evidence, including the data presented here, suggests a model where progenitor cells give rise to a clone of sister M/T cells that migrate throughout the olfactory bulb such that sister cells disperse independently from each, and their cell bodies do not end up close to each other in specific regions of the bulb.

source: After neuronal migration is completed, immature M/T cells initially grow multiple dendrites that receive synaptic input from multiple glomeruli without any apparent specificity.

source: Finally, it is curious that the targeting of OSN axons and M/T dendrites toward the glomeruli appears to be regulated by very different mechanisms.

source: These experiments suggest that the targeting of OSN axons into the OB to form glomeruli does not require the presence of M/T cells.

source: However, the connectivity between M/T cells and the amygdala appears to be more stereotypical than between the M/T cells and other targets in the olfactory cortex (anterior olfactory nucleus, piriform cortex, tenia tecta, olfactory tubercle, cortical amygdala and entorhinal cortex) (Haberly, 2001; Sosulski et al., 2011).

claim: The connectivity between the OB and its targets in the olfactory cortex may occur by two different mechanisms: genetic factors (including lineage) may contribute to the connectivity between M/T cells and the amygdala, while the connectivity between M/T cells and areas of the olfactory cortex involved in the perception of odors that do not elicit innate behaviors are more plastic and may be regulated by mechanisms independent of lineage.
source: Based on these observations, one can speculate that the connectivity between the OB and its targets in the olfactory cortex may occur by two different mechanisms. Genetic factors, including lineage, may contribute to the connectivity between M/T cells and the amygdala, as this brain area is involved in innate behavior responses that may require hardwired connections (Sosulski et al., 2011). In contrast, the connectivity between M/T cells and areas of the olfactory cortex involved in the perception of odors that do not elicit innate behaviors are more plastic and may be regulated by mechanisms independent of lineage, such as random neurite targeting and activity-dependent wiring, among others (Caron et al., 2013; Schaffer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative model proposed by the authors based on prior work.
